passages.t: Zedekiah asks for a wonder, and the way of life and death
passages.happening:
King Zedekiah sends Pashhur son of Malchijah and the priest Zephaniah to Jeremiah (verse 1). They ask him to inquire of the LORD, since Nebuchadnezzar is making war on them. Perhaps the LORD will work one of his wonders, they say, and make the king of Babylon withdraw (verse 2).

Jeremiah's answer is the opposite. God will turn back the weapons in their hands and gather the enemy into the city (verse 4). ‘And I Myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand and a mighty arm, with anger, fury, and great wrath’ (verse 5). Plague will strike the city, and then Zedekiah and the survivors will be handed to Nebuchadnezzar, who will show no pity (verses 6 and 7).

To the people God says, ‘Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death’ (verse 8). Whoever stays in the city will die by sword, famine and plague, but whoever goes out and surrenders to the Chaldeans will live (verse 9). God has set his face against the city for harm and not good, and it will be burned (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Zedekiah, a son of Josiah, was put on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar in 597 BC after his nephew Jehoiachin was taken away. He ruled as Babylon's subject but rebelled, and Babylon's army besieged Jerusalem from the ninth year of his reign. This chapter belongs to that siege.

Kings in the ancient world routinely sought a prophet's word before or during a war. Zedekiah's request was ordinary. The answer was shocking. The words outstretched hand and mighty arm were the words used of the exodus, when God fought for Israel against Egypt. Now God would use them against his own city.

The way of life and the way of death echoes Moses' last words in Deuteronomy, where life meant loving and obeying God. Here, at the end, life meant surrender.
passages.later: Moses had set the same choice before Israel: ‘See, I have set before you today life and goodness, as well as death and disaster’ (Deuteronomy 30:15). Kings records the siege: ‘Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched against Jerusalem with his entire army’ (2 Kings 25:1).
passages.hard:
Was Jeremiah a traitor for telling his own people to surrender to the enemy?

His contemporaries thought so. The officials later demanded his death because his words weakened the soldiers' morale (38:4), and he was arrested on suspicion of deserting (37:13-14). From a purely political point of view, a public figure urging surrender during a siege is dangerous. Jeremiah's answer was that he was not serving Babylon but speaking what God had said: the city's fall was decided as judgment for its broken covenant, and those who went out would live. He did not hate his people; he wept over them (9:1) and chose to stay with the remnant in Judah after the fall (40:1-6).

His message rested on a direct word from God about one judgment at one time. It is not a general rule that God's people should surrender to every enemy, and these notes draw no line from it to any nation or war of the present day.
passages.asks: Zedekiah wanted a wonder without a change of heart. Ask whether you have asked God to rescue you while refusing to listen to him. And ask what it would take for you to choose the way of life when it looks like defeat.

passages.t: Do justice every morning, house of David
passages.happening:
Jeremiah speaks to the royal house. They must ‘Administer justice every morning, and rescue the victim of robbery from the hand of his oppressor’ (verse 12), or God's wrath will break out like fire because of their evil deeds (verse 12).

God is against the city that sits above the valley on its rocky plateau, which says no one can come against it or enter its dwellings (verse 13). He will punish them as their deeds deserve and kindle a fire in their forest that will consume everything around it (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Justice every morning means the king's daily work of hearing cases at the gate. Morning was the time for judgment, while the day was fresh. The king's first duty was to rescue those who had been robbed.

Jerusalem sat on a ridge with valleys on three sides, and it felt safe. Its people believed no one could break in. God says the very height they trust in will not save them.
passages.later: A psalm of the king says, ‘Every morning I will remove all the wicked of the land’ (Psalm 101:8). The next chapter carries the same word to each of Judah's kings (Jeremiah 22:3).
passages.asks: The king's first work each morning was to rescue the robbed. Ask what your first work each day says about what matters to you. And ask what height or safety you trust that God might be against.
